source_text: Ὁ μὲν οὖν Ἰησοῦς ἐπιστρέφων τοὺς μαθητὰς οὐχὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ [μὴ] προσέχειν ἁπαξαπλῶς γόησι καὶ τοῖς ἐπαγγελλομένοις δι᾿ οἱασδήποτε ὁδοῦ ποιεῖν τεράστια (οὐ γὰρ ἐδέοντο τούτου οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ) ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ τοῦ τοῖς ἀναγορεύουσιν ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι τὸν Χριστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πειρωμένοις διά τινων φαντασιῶν πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιστρέφειν τοὺς Ἰησοῦ μαθητὰς ὅπου μὲν εἶπε· „τότε ἐάν τις ὑμῖν εἴπῃ· ἰδοὺ ὧδε ὁ Χριστὸς ἢ ὧδε, μὴ πιστεύετε. ἐγερθήσονται γὰρ ψευδόχριστοι καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται καὶ δώσουσι σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα μεγάλα. ὥστε πλανᾶσθαι εἰ δυνατὸν καὶ τοὺς ἐκλεκτούς. ἰδοὺ προείρηκα ὑμῖν. ἐὰν οὖν εἴπωσιν ὑμῖν· ἰδοὺ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ἐστὶ, μὴ ἐξέλθητε· ἰδοὺ ἐν τοῖς ταμείοις, μὴ πιστεύσητε. ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ ἀστραπὴ ἐξέρχεται ἀπ᾿ ἀνατολῶν καὶ φαίνεται ἕως δυσμῶν, οὕτως ἔσται ἡ παρουσία τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου“· ὅπου δέ· „πολλοὶ ἐροῦσί μοι ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ· κύριε, κύριε, οὐ τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἐφάγομεν καὶ τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἐπίομεν καὶ τῷ ὀνόματί σου δαιμόνια ἐξεβάλομεν καὶ δυνάμεις πολλὰς ἐποιήσαμεν; καὶ ἐρῶ αὐτοῖς· ἀποχωρεῖτε ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ. ὅτι ἐστὲ ἐργάται ἀδικίας.“ ὁ δὲ Κέλσος κοινοποιῆσαι βουλόμενος τὰ τεράστια τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πρὸς τὴν ἐν ἀνθρώποις γοητείαν φησὶν αὐταῖς λέξεσιν· ὦ φῶς καὶ ἀλήθεια, τῇ αὐτοῦ φωνῇ διαῤῥήδην ἐξαγορεύει, καθὰ καὶ ὑμεῖς συγγεγράφατε, διότι παρέσονται ὑμῖν καὶ ἕτεροι δυνάμεσιν ὁμοίαις χρώμενοι, κακοὶ καὶ γόητες, καὶ σατανᾶν τινα τοιαῦτα παραμηχανώμενον ὀνομάζει· ᾥστ᾿ οὐδὲ αὐτὸς ἔξαρνός ἐστιν, ὡς ταῦτά γε οὐδὲν θεῖον ἀλλὰ πονηρῶν ἐστιν ἔργα. βιαζόμενος δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας ὁμοῦ καὶ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἀπεκάλυψε καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ αὑτὸν ἤλεγξε. πῶς οὖν οὐ σχέτλιον ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ἔργων τὸν μὲν θεὸν τοὺς δὲ γόητας ἡγεῖσθαι; τί γὰρ μᾶλλον ἀπό γε τούτων τοὺς ἄλλους πονηροὺς ἢ τοῦτον νομιστέον αὐτῷ χρωμένους μάρτυρι; ταῦτα μέν γε καὶ αὐτὸς ὡμολόγησεν οὐχὶ θείας φύσεως ἀλλ᾿ ἀπατεώνων τινῶν καὶ παμπονήρων εἶναι γνωρίσματα. ὅρα δὴ εἰ μὴ ἐν τούτοις σαφῶς ὁ Κέλσος ἐλέγχεται κακουργῶν τὸν λόγον, ἄλλο μὲν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ λέγοντος περὶ τῶν ποιησόντων „σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα,“ ἄλλο δὲ τοῦ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαίου φάσκοντος. καὶ γὰρ εἰ μὲν ἁπλῶς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἔλεγεν Ἰησοῦς φυλάσσεσθαι τοὺς τὰ τεράστια ἐπαγγελλομένους οὐ παρατιθέμενος, τί φήσουσιν ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι, τάχα χώραν εἶχεν ἂν ἡ ὑπόνοια αὐτοῦ· ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἀφ᾿ ὧν θέλει ἡμᾶς φυλάσσεσθαι ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐπαγγέλλονται εἶναι „ὁ Χριστὸς,“ ὅπερ οὐ ποιοῦσιν οἱ γόητες, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ βιοῦντας κακῶς φησι τινὰς δυνάμεις ποιήσειν καὶ δαίμονας ἀποβαλεῖν ἀνθρώπων· μᾶλλον δ᾿, εἰ δεῖ οὕτως εἰπεῖν, ἀποκηρύσσεται μὲν τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἡ γοητεία καὶ πᾶσα ἡ κατ᾿ αὐτῶν ὑπόνοια, εἰσάγεται δὲ ἡ θειότης τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ θειότης τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, ὅτι δυνατόν τινα τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ χρησάμενον καὶ οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ἐνεργηθέντα ὑπό τινος δυνάμεως πρὸς τὸ προσποιήσασθαι, ὅτι αὐτὸς εἴη ὁ Χριστὸς, δοκεῖν τὰ παραπλήσια ἐπιτελεῖν τῷ Χριστῷ καὶ ἄλλους τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τὰ ὡσπερεὶ παραπλήσια τοῖς γνησίοις αὐτοῦ μαθηταῖς.
pass_a_gloss: The Jesus, turning back the disciples, not from the not paying attention simply to magicians and to the ones promising through some way to do great things (for the disciples of Him were not in need of this) but from the ones proclaiming themselves to be the Christ of God and attempting through some fantasies to turn back the disciples of Jesus to themselves, where He said: 'Then if someone says to you: Behold, here is the Christ or there, do not believe. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and will give great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect. Behold, I have told you beforehand. If therefore they say to you: Behold, He is in the wilderness, do not go out; behold, He is in the inner rooms, do not believe. For just as the lightning comes out from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.' And where: 'Many will say to me in that day: Lord, Lord, did we not eat in your name and drink in your name and cast out demons in your name and do many mighty works? And I will say to them: Depart from me, for you are workers of lawlessness.' But Celsus, wanting to make common the great things of Jesus with the sorcery among men, says to them in these words: 'O light and truth, with his own voice he openly proclaims, as you also have written, that there will be others who will come with similar powers, evil and sorcerers, and some Satan will devise such things.' Therefore, he is not without guilt, as if these things are not divine but works of evil ones. But being forced by the truth, he has revealed both the things of others and examined the things concerning himself. How then is it not absurd to consider the one God and the others sorcerers from the same works? For what more than these should the others, evil ones, be thought to use as a witness for themselves? These things, indeed, he himself has acknowledged are not of a divine nature but of certain deceivers and thoroughly evil ones. See, then, if Celsus is not clearly convicted of evil-doing in these things, saying one thing about the things Jesus said concerning those who will do 'signs and wonders' and another thing about what the Jew according to Celsus says. And if Jesus were simply telling the disciples to beware of those promising great things without specifying what they claim to be, perhaps his suspicion would have some place. But since Jesus wants us to beware of those who promise to be 'the Christ', which sorcerers do not do, but also says that some living badly in the name of Jesus will do powers and cast out demons of men, rather, if one must say so, the sorcery of those in the place is proclaimed and every suspicion concerning them is introduced, but the divinity of Christ and the divinity of His disciples is introduced, because it is possible for someone using His name, and I do not know how, being energized by some power, to seem to accomplish similar things to Christ, and others, in the name of Jesus, to do things similar to His genuine disciples.

pass_b_english: Jesus turned his disciples away, not from merely paying attention to magicians and those who promise to perform wonders by some method or other (the disciples had no need of that warning), but from those who proclaim themselves to be God's Christ and try, through fantasies of their own making, to lure Jesus' disciples back to themselves. He warned them in two passages. In the first he said: "If anyone tells you, 'Look, here is the Messiah!' or 'There he is!' do not believe it. False messiahs and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect. I have told you beforehand. So if they say to you, 'Look, he is in the wilderness,' do not go out; 'Look, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it. For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man" (Matthew 24:23-24, 26-27). In the second he said: "Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not eat in your name and drink in your name and cast out demons in your name and do many mighty works?' And I will tell them, 'Depart from me, for you are workers of lawlessness'" (Matthew 7:22-23).

Celsus, wanting to assimilate Jesus' mighty works to the sorcery practiced among people, quotes him in these very words: "O Light and Truth, with his own voice he openly proclaims, as you also have written, that others will come to you using similar powers, evil men and sorcerers, and he names some Satan as the one devising such things." By this reasoning Celsus makes himself guilty, as though these works were not divine but the deeds of evil agents. Yet, compelled by the truth, he has disclosed both what others do and has brought his own position under scrutiny. How, then, is it not absurd to judge the one as God and the others as sorcerers on the basis of the same works? For what stronger witness could the others, who are evil, possibly invoke for themselves than these very works? Celsus himself has conceded that these things are not marks of a divine nature but tokens of certain deceivers and thoroughly wicked men.

Consider, then, whether Celsus is not clearly convicted of distorting the argument here. Jesus speaks one way about those who will perform "signs and wonders," while the Jew in Celsus's dialogue says something quite different. If Jesus had merely told his disciples to beware of those who promise great things without specifying what they claim to be, Celsus's suspicion might have had some foothold. But Jesus warns us to beware of those who promise to be "the Christ" — a claim sorcerers do not make — and he also says that some who live wickedly in his name will perform powers and cast out demons. Rather, if one must put it this way, the sorcery of those in that camp and every suspicion attached to them are exposed for what they are, while the divinity of Christ and the divinity of his disciples are affirmed. For it is possible that someone, using his name — I do not know how — may be energized by some power to appear to accomplish works similar to Christ's, and that others, in the name of Jesus, may do things resembling those of his genuine disciples.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the parenthetical clarification regarding the disciples' needs and the distinction between the sorcery of the deceivers and the divinity of Christ/disciples. Scripture citations in Pass B (Matthew 24:23-24, 26-27 and Matthew 7:22-23) correctly identify the quoted/alluded passages in the Greek text.
